html:
A merchant ship that sank off Uluburun, near Kaş on the south coast of Turkey, in the late 1300s BCE. Found by a sponge diver in 1982 and excavated over eleven seasons, it is the richest Late Bronze Age wreck known.

The ship was about 15 metres long and carried over 20 tons of cargo. Most of it was raw metal: some ten tons of copper, mostly in "oxhide" ingots from Cyprus, and about a ton of tin, the right mix to make bronze. There were also ingots of blue glass, Canaanite jars of resin, ebony, ivory, ostrich eggs, Baltic amber, and a gold scarab bearing the name of Nefertiti.

The goods came from at least seven cultures, from Egypt and the Canaanite coast to Mycenaean Greece and Mesopotamia. The wreck shows how linked the Bronze Age Mediterranean was, with royal gift exchange and trade side by side. A century later that network broke in the Late Bronze Age collapse.
